title: PBOC is expected to set the USD/CNY reference rate at 6.6758 – Reuters estimate
body: The People's Bank of China is due to set the daily USD/CNY reference rate at around 0115 GMT (2115 US Eastern time), a fixing that remains one of the most closely watched signals in Asian foreign exchange markets. China operates a managed floating exchange rate system, under which the renminbi (yuan) is allowed to trade within a prescribed band around a central reference rate, or midpoint, set each trading day by the PBOC. The current trading band permits the currency to move plus or minus 2% from the official midpoint during onshore trading hours. Each morning, the PBOC determines the midpoint based on a range of inputs. These include the previous day's closing price, movements in major currencies, particularly the US dollar, broader international FX conditions, and domestic economic considerations such as capital flows, growth momentum and financial stability objectives. The midpoint is not a purely mechanical calculation, allowing policymakers discretion to guide market expectations. Once the midpoint is announced, onshore USD/CNY is free to trade within the allowable band. If market pressures push the yuan toward either edge of that range, the central bank may step in to smooth volatility. Intervention can take the form of direct buying or selling of yuan, adjustments to liquidity conditions, or guidance through state-owned banks. As a result, the daily fixing is often interpreted as a policy signal rather than just a technical reference point.

title: What is blockchain finality? Why Bitcoin, Ethereum and Solana settle at very different speeds
body: When you send Bitcoin, Ether or SOL, the transaction shows up almost immediately. That doesn't mean it is permanent. Every blockchain has a point after which a transaction can no longer be reversed, called finality, and the time it takes to get there ranges from under a second to around an hour depending on the network. Solana's Alpenglow upgrade this week cut its finality time from about 12.8 seconds to a target of roughly 150 milliseconds, which makes this a good moment to explain what finality is and why traders should care. What finality means A blockchain is a shared record kept by thousands of computers that must agree on which transactions happened and in what order. Agreement takes time. Until enough of the network has signed off, there is a small chance a transaction could be dropped or replaced if part of the network had a different view of events. Finality is the point where that chance is gone, or so small it can be ignored. Before it, a transaction is pending, however confident the screen looks. After it, the transaction is settled. Bitcoin: finality by accumulation Bitcoin never declares a transaction final. Instead, each new block added on top makes it harder to reverse, because rewriting history would mean redoing all the computing work in those later blocks. New blocks arrive about every 10 minutes on average. This is called probabilistic finality. The longer you wait, the safer the transaction becomes.

title: Solana's Alpenglow upgrade cuts settlement to under a second: what it changes, and what it doesn't, for SOL
body: Solana switched on its Alpenglow upgrade on Wednesday, 21 October, replacing the consensus system the network has run since its 2020 launch. The headline change is speed. Transactions now reach finality, the point where they can no longer be reversed, in a fraction of a second instead of roughly 12.8 seconds. That is a real improvement for exchanges, payment apps and traders using the network. Whether it creates more demand for SOL itself is a separate question, and the early price action suggests the market sees it that way. What happened Anza, the firm behind Agave, Solana's main validator software, scheduled the switch for about 14:50 UTC. The feature activated at the start of epoch 1064. The old system, TowerBFT, kept running for another 5,000 slots, roughly 18 minutes, before handing over to Alpenglow at slot 459,653,000. The network did not restart. Anza described it as swapping consensus engines on a live network. Validators approved the upgrade in September 2025, with about 98% voting in favour. Alpenglow went live on Solana's testnet on 24 September this year and on devnet a day later. Before the mainnet date was set, Anza ran a bug bounty of more than 25,000 SOL, drew on work from 115 security researchers, and simulated the network across 1,500 nodes. An earlier September target came and went, with developers saying publicly they would not rush it. Why finality matters A blockchain confirms transactions in stages.

title: Macro pulse: Europe's economy is losing steam but inflation won't let up
body: The latest October PMI readings today don't paint a particularly encouraging picture of the health of the euro area economy. Growth is slowing and businesses are feeling the pinch, but inflation pressures are still refusing to go away. And that is the sort of headache that the ECB really doesn't need right now. The data showed disappointing readings from both the manufacturing and services sectors, with the latter slowing rather markedly. A lot of that can be attributed to France though, as business activity there returned to contraction in October. And while Germany continues to hold up better, the broader slowdown across the region is becoming more difficult to ignore as we look to the final quarter this year. With that in mind, this is where things get uncomfortable for the ECB. While business activity are showing signs of slowing down, price pressures haven't quite followed suit. In looking at the chart above, businesses are still grappling with elevated cost pressures. The report noted that manufacturers saw a sharp acceleration in input prices in October, largely driven by higher energy costs, with the latest increase being the steepest since May. The only consolation to this is that output price inflation did at least ease a little on the month. However, that could also be hinting that businesses may be finding it harder to pass rising costs on to consumers. So, that is all leaving the ECB with quite the dilemma.

title: Crude oil extends gains as Saudi-Houthi conflict and concerns of US-Iran attacks keep the market supported
body: The bullish momentum in crude oil has been slowly picking up after The New York Times reported that the US and Israeli militaries had developed plans for renewed strikes on Iran following the US midterm elections, with additional forces expected to be fully deployed by early November. The Saudi-Houthi conflict, meanwhile, continues with the Houthis recently targeting Saudi airports and energy infrastructure, including a reported strike near Dammam that killed two people and injured eight. Saudi Aramco instructed staff to evacuate its Dhahran headquarters and work remotely following the latest security incidents. The attacks in the Strait of Hormuz have intensified recently after Iran said in early October that it would close illegal routes used by the US to escort vessels through the strait. The IRGC claimed yesterday that it attacked four vessels and three others struck naval mines. This morning, Iran claimed that the illicit vessel traffic in Hormuz stopped after the continued attacks. Looking ahead, crude oil remains supported amid the tensions in the Middle East and the prospects of another US attack against Iran after the midterms. Unless we get a de-escalation in the Saudi-Houthi conflict or a surprising breakthrough in US-Iran negotiations, oil prices will likely continue to rise.

title: Gold gets caught in market liquidation despite falling real yields supporting higher prices
body: Gold extended the losses yesterday after breaking below the 4,070 support as widespread risk aversion tightened financial conditions. It looks like gold have been driven mainly by liquidations to cover losses in the stock market, much like what we've seen in 2025. To understand the mechanics, imagine that an investment fund holds stocks, gold and government bonds. Some stocks suddenly crash, and the fund suffers losses on leveraged positions. The fund may need to raise cash to meet margin calls, reduce leverage or satisfy investor redemptions. Rather than selling only the assets that caused the losses, it may sell whatever it can liquidate quickly. Gold is particularly useful in this situation because it is highly liquid and can be sold quickly. The main drivers like real yields have been actually pointing to higher gold prices. In fact, real yields fell significantly as inflation expectations remain roughly unchanged given the increase in oil prices, while nominal Treasury yields fell due to growth concerns. This might be an opportunity for the buyers to fade the weakness and enter at better prices. Today, the focus will be on the US Flash PMIs. If the data surprises to the downside, growth concerns will likely intensify, and we should get another dovish repricing. In this scenario, gold should be supported as real yields would fall further. Stronger than expected data, on the other hand, could quell growth fears in the near-term and put renewed pressure on gold.

title: Eurozone October PMI misses estimates as growth slows, keeping ECB rate hike dilemma alive
body: Eurozone October flash services PMI 51.7 vs 52.5 expected Prior 53.0 Eurozone October flash manufacturing PMI 52.4 vs 52.7 expected Prior 52.9 Eurozone October flash composite PMI 51.9 vs 52.7 expected Prior 53.1 After the softer prints from France and Germany, the weaker-than-expected results for the overall euro area are not all too surprising. But at least for now, business activity continues to grow with both output and new orders increasing for the fourth successive month in October, albeit at the slowest pace during this sequence. A key drag on growth was a renewed drop in business activity in the French services sector. But there were also signs of weakness elsewhere in the region as growth also edged lower in the rest of the euro area for both the manufacturing and services sectors. Looking to prices, manufacturers reported a sharp and accelerated increase in input prices in October amid higher energy costs mostly. The latest rise was the steepest since May and above the average for the year-to-date. However, the rate of output price inflation slowed in October at least with both Germany and France posting weaker increases in selling prices than in September. As for the rest of the euro area, they saw the rate of inflation accelerate as a whole. Overall, the data pretty much underscores that higher interest rates are also starting to take a toll and dampening demand.

title: France October PMI slumps back into contraction as political uncertainty weighs on demand
body: France October flash services PMI 48.4 vs 50.7 expected Prior 51.2 France October flash manufacturing PMI 49.3 vs 50.5 expected Prior 50.6 France October flash composite PMI 48.4 vs 50.5 expected Prior 51.1 That's not a good sign as the French private sector falls back into contraction in October, amid political and financial concerns. Weighing on activity levels was the sharpest decline in demand for French goods and services since May, which surveyed businesses attributed to heightened uncertainty and economic pressures. The only good news perhaps for the ECB is that the survey's price gauges decreased from September to signal an easing of input cost and output charge inflation rates. Looking at the breakdown, manufacturers and service providers reported steeper declines in demand amid reports of projects being postponed as customers held back on decision making. Meanwhile, French businesses turned pessimistic towards one-year outlook with the future composite index falling to its lowest level since April 2020. That indicates negative corporate sentiment for the first time in close to two years. The more downbeat expectations were often linked to next year's election period, with some companies also expressing concerns regarding public finances. On prices, data at the composite level signalled an easing of inflation across France in October.

body: Prior 53.9 Services PMI 51.7 vs 52.5 expected Prior 52.9 Composite PMI 52.8 vs 53.3 expected Prior 53.8 Key findings: Economic activity softens in October Comment: Phil Smith, Economics Associate Director at S&P Global Market Intelligence: "October's flash PMI results encouragingly showed a sustained upturn in business activity across Germany, although a slowdown in growth underscored that the recovery in the eurozone's largest economy remains fragile. Inflows of new work rose only modestly and at the slowest rate for three months at the start of the fourth quarter, with a stalling of new business growth in the service sector highlighting the ongoing headwinds to demand from elevated inflation and uncertainty. "Labour market conditions continue to show a very gradual improvement, reflecting a steady but modest pace of job creation among services providers alongside an increasingly stable picture in the manufacturing sector. "Whilst goods producers continued to see business conditions improve, aided by sustained growth in export sales and the filtering through of increased defence and infrastructure spending, a renewed surge in cost pressures has dampened expectations across the sector, with the two likely to remain intrinsically linked in the months ahead." title: UK retail sales fall more than expected in September, complicating BOE rate hike outlook
body: UK September retail sales -0.4% vs -0.1% m/m expected Prior +0.5; revised to +0.7% UK September retail sales +0.8% vs +1.0% y/y expected Prior +2.4%; revised to +2.7% UK September retail sales (ex autos, fuel) -0.7% vs -0.1% m/m expected Prior +0.6%; revised to +0.9% UK September retail sales (ex autos, fuel) +0.8% vs +1.5% y/y expected Prior +2.7%; revised to +2.9% UK retail sales disappointed in September, falling by 0.4% on the month and missing expectations of a 0.1% decline. That comes after a stronger revision to the August number, which saw a 0.7% increase. Having said that, the quarterly picture is still holding up reasonably well as retail sales volumes rose by 0.7% in Q3 compared with the previous quarter. Looking at the details, the weakness was fairly broad. Supermarket sales declined after gains in the previous two months, while non-food store sales volumes fell by 0.4%. Clothing retailers also struggled, with the unusually warm September weather weighing on demand for autumn and winter collections. However, there are also signs that consumers are becoming more cautious with some retailers pointing to lower footfall and customers cutting back on spending. Coming into the report, markets have been pricing in roughly 98% odds of a November rate hike, with December sitting closer to 45%. The numbers today will not do much to derail expectations for November, especially after the recent inflation figures.

title: Falling Treasury yields may be hiding a darker story about the AI boom
body: Let's take a step back and check on the key market drivers this week. The US-Iran conflict is still raging on and geopolitical tensions remain high. So, that is underpinning oil prices once again with WTI crude breaching $100 and Brent crude hitting $114 - its highest since May. Now, that sounds like a familiar backdrop for the bond market, doesn't it? Higher oil prices mean stronger inflation pressures, which should normally push up Treasury yields. Well, that has not been the case this week. Instead, Treasury yields have fallen sharply, with 10-year yields even slipping back below the 5% threshold in overnight trading and holding thereabouts since. But wait a second, shouldn't falling yields then buy some relief for stocks? You would certainly think so, especially when surging Treasury yields have been such a major bane for equities over the past two months. And yet stocks have been battered this week, with AI names in particular bearing the brunt of the pain. So, what gives? It's one thing to suggest that investors are perhaps starting to worry about growth conditions again. title: Sensex Finishes Week Lower
body: India's BSE Sensex slipped about 0.2% on Friday to a more than one-week low of 73,124, extending its losing streak to a fourth consecutive session and closing the week 2.1% lower. Sentiment remained under pressure amid concerns over rising crude oil prices, escalating geopolitical tensions, and uncertainty about the broader global outlook. Elevated oil prices threaten to widen India's import bill, worsen the inflation trajectory, and squeeze corporate profit margins. Foreign institutional investors also added to the downside, offloading Indian equities worth 3.46 billion rupees on October 22. title: WP - 2026-10-23 - Severin Joho and Enzo Rossi: The evolution of frequency, language complexity and policy narrative: benchmarking Python-based NLP and ChatGPT on a century of SNB rhetoric
body: We compiled and processed a novel, comprehensive dataset of 1,063 speeches delivered by high-ranking Swiss National Bank officials between 1928 and 2024. Beyond tracking their quantitative evolution, we conducted an in-depth analysis of the length, readability and thematic content. To ensure robust results, we benchmarked traditional Python-based NLP text mining against generative artificial intelligence using ChatGPT. Our findings highlight four primary policy insights. First, the frequency of annual speeches has followed an upward trajectory since the mid-1950s, accelerating notably after the transition to flexible exchange rates. Second, a clear shift toward brevity is evident. Third, the language has become increasingly accessible since the 1960s. Fourth, inflation has moved to the forefront of the thematic discourse in the era of flexible exchange rates, while cyclical economic development and unemployment have received less emphasis. Finally, we outline key methodological lessons for deploying LLMs to analyze central bank communication, emphasizing the complementary relationship between probabilistic language models and deterministic Python frameworks, while addressing inherent algorithmic pitfalls and identifying critical open questions for future research.
